summary: Argues for active protocol maintenance, evolving specifications and implementations over time to reduce ambiguity and keep protocols interoperable. It reexamines the robustness principle, being conservative in what you send and liberal in what you accept.

eli5.summary: Rules for a game should be updated as people find confusing spots, so everyone keeps playing the same game.

subtitle: Evolving specifications and implementations to preserve long-term protocol interoperability.

tldr.problem: The robustness principle—"be conservative in what you send, liberal in what you accept"—was designed for early Internet development, but tolerating ambiguous or faulty inputs leads to protocol decay, divergent implementations, and interoperability problems over time.
tldr.mechanism: Active protocol maintenance means protocol designers, implementers, and operators work together to evolve specifications and deployments in concert. When discrepancies are found, the community updates both specifications and implementations rather than adding workarounds.
tldr.outcome: Protocols remain cleanly specified and consistently implemented across the ecosystem, avoiding the pitfall where faulty implementations become de facto standards that new implementations must replicate to interoperate.

today: RFC 9413 is an informational document from the Internet Architecture Board published in June 2023. It represents consensus guidance from the IAB on best practices for protocol stewardship. The document had broad but not unanimous approval, with some concerns expressed about how broadly the guidance applies in all situations. Nevertheless, it serves as the authoritative modern articulation of how to maintain protocol health in the long term.

sections.title: The Robustness Principle and Its Limits
sections.content:
The robustness principle, stated in RFC 1958, advises: "Be strict when sending and tolerant when receiving." This meant implementations should follow specifications precisely when sending data, but gracefully handle unexpected or faulty input without crashing. The principle was instrumental in the early Internet's success, where protocols were imperfect and implementation experience was invaluable.

However, modern interpretation of robustness—particularly the third aspect, tolerating unexpected inputs—can be harmful. While robustness against software defects and attacks remains essential, silently accepting faulty input masks problems instead of solving them. Specifications are indeed imperfect, but the solution is not to tolerate ambiguity indefinitely; it is to evolve specifications and implementations together.
sections.eli5: Robustness used to mean: ignore weird stuff and keep going. That worked when protocols were new. Now it means: fix the weird stuff together.

sections.title: How Tolerating Errors Causes Protocol Decay
sections.content:
When one implementation deviates from a specification—whether due to a bug, ambiguity, or performance pressure—and other implementations tolerate that deviation to interoperate, a feedback loop begins. Over time, the errant behavior becomes entrenched. Later implementations must replicate it to achieve interoperability, even though it contradicts the specification. This is called being "bug-for-bug compatible."

The RFC provides concrete examples: in TLS, some server implementations incorrectly rejected ClientHello messages ending with an empty extension. Client implementations were forced to add workarounds, padding ClientHello messages to avoid the empty extension, even though the specification allowed it. Each workaround makes implementations more complex, harder to maintain, and harder for new implementations to join the ecosystem. The flaw becomes a de facto standard, and the specification becomes increasingly irrelevant.
sections.eli5: If one player cheats and others let them, everyone else has to cheat the same way. Pretty soon, cheating is the rule and the real rules are forgotten.

sections.title: The Ecosystem Consequences of Lax Tolerance
sections.content:
Protocol ecosystems have two stable states: strict compliance or widespread tolerance. If implementations are strict, newer implementations face immediate feedback on any non-compliance and must fix it. If implementations are tolerant, non-compliant implementations deploy successfully, and new implementations feel pressure to tolerate the same non-compliance. The ecosystem converges toward tolerance, but at a cost: interoperability becomes dependent on reverse-engineering deployed implementations rather than reading the specification.

This creates high barriers for new implementations. A new implementation must discover and replicate all the undocumented quirks of existing implementations to achieve interoperability. At scale, these quirks are impossible to fully discover. The cost of building a new implementation rises, and new implementations become restricted to niche use cases. This hurts protocol evolution: new implementations often bring new ideas and capabilities that benefit the entire ecosystem, but when they cannot interoperate, they fork the protocol instead.
sections.eli5: If everyone's sloppy, everyone else has to be sloppy too. If everyone's strict, new players have an easy time. Lax tolerance makes it hard for anyone new to join the game.

sections.title: Active Protocol Maintenance as the Solution
sections.content:
Active protocol maintenance is the practice of ongoing collaboration among protocol designers, implementers, and operators to improve and evolve protocols alongside their deployments. When an implementer discovers a discrepancy between a specification and deployed implementations, the community gathers to understand the root cause: is the specification ambiguous? Is it wrong? Are implementations buggy?

Through consensus, the community updates the specification to clarify intent or correct errors, and implementers update their code to match the evolved specification. This requires the ability to deploy updates, which is increasingly feasible with modern software update mechanisms. Early implementations have a stronger obligation to follow the specification precisely, because their behavior will influence all subsequent implementations. Later implementations can more readily use deployed implementations as a guide, but only if early ones were strict.
sections.eli5: Active maintenance means when someone finds a problem, the group fixes it together instead of working around it.

sections.title: Virtuous Intolerance: Using Strictness Constructively
sections.content:
Virtuous intolerance means generating fatal errors for unspecified or invalid conditions, rather than attempting error recovery or silent discard. When a new implementation encounters a peer that is intolerant of an error, it receives clear, immediate feedback. This allows problems to be discovered and fixed quickly during development rather than accumulating in deployed versions.

For virtuous intolerance to work, multiple implementations must deploy strict checks so that new implementations encounter them with high probability. Error messages must be informative and reach people who can fix them. Stateless protocols that cannot authenticate senders must be careful not to generate denial-of-service vulnerabilities by responding to every malformed message. When intolerance is combined with well-specified error handling, it becomes a tool for improving the entire ecosystem.
sections.eli5: If you immediately reject bad input instead of ignoring it, the person sending bad input finds out and can fix their code.

sections.title: Security, Exclusion, and Protocol Evolution
sections.content:
Active maintenance enables deliberate exclusion: when security concerns or interoperability problems require breaking compatibility with existing deployments, the community can make an intentional choice. For example, weak cryptographic primitives or obsolete mechanisms can be excluded via specification updates and enforcement in implementations. This is far healthier than the alternative: maintaining support for unsafe practices indefinitely.

The RFC acknowledges that exclusion carries risks. Changing a protocol can break existing deployments that cannot or will not update. However, maintaining broken interoperability indefinitely is often worse. Good protocol maintenance includes migration planning: understanding the affected deployments, providing advance notice, and giving them time to update. This approach has been used successfully to deprecate unsafe cryptography in TLS and to evolve other critical protocols. The key is intention and communication, not drift.
sections.eli5: Sometimes you have to say: this old way doesn't work anymore, everyone must switch. If you plan ahead and give people time, it works better than letting bad things continue.
